category_name: Nutrition, swallowing, hydration and mouth care

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'count something nobody counts' produced a daily count of cups actually finished, and 'a daughter' set the carer viewpoint; envelope, house removals, pruning, delay and the first week gave nothing usable.
candidates.working_title: Count the cups, not the thirst
candidates.core_insight: Thirst is a weak guide to how much an older person needs to drink, so counting the cups they actually finish tells a carer more than asking whether they are thirsty.
candidates.angle: Replace the question 'are you thirsty?' with a simple daily tally of cups finished, checked against an amount agreed with the GP or nurse. In a UK care home study, thirst was not associated with whether a resident was dehydrated.
candidates.position: For older people at risk of drinking too little, carers should track cups finished each day rather than rely on thirst. The target should be set individually when heart or kidney conditions limit fluids. This is practical advice built on physiology and observational data, not a trial finding.
claims_needing_evidence: After 24 hours without water, healthy men aged 67 to 75 felt less thirsty and drank less than young men (small physiology study; Phillips 1984).

In UK long-term care (DRIE, 188 residents, mean age 86, excluding heart and kidney failure), about 1 in 5 were dehydrated by serum osmolality over 300 mOsm/kg, and thirst was not associated with hydration status (cohort study; Hooper 2016).
ESPEN recommends that older women drink at least 1.6 litres and older men at least 2.0 litres a day unless a clinical condition requires otherwise (guideline full text needed to confirm wording).
Missing drinks between meals was one of the few signs with some ability to detect dehydration, in one small study (Cochrane diagnostic review; Hooper 2015).
Any cup-count target shown needs a stated cup volume from a source, or must be labelled as an illustrative example.
evidence_leads: Phillips PA et al. Reduced thirst after water deprivation in healthy elderly men. N Engl J Med 1984;311:753-9. PMID 6472364 (abstract read on PubMed in this session: 7 older and 7 young men).

Hooper L et al. Which frail older people are dehydrated? The UK DRIE study. J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci 2016;71:1341-7. PMID 26553658 (abstract read on PubMed in this session: 20% dehydrated; thirst not associated with hydration status).

Volkert D et al. ESPEN guideline on clinical nutrition and hydration in geriatrics. Clin Nutr 2019;38:10-47 (drink volumes to confirm in full text; abstract content also appears in a 2026 Spanish translation, PMID 41820196).

Hooper L et al. Clinical symptoms, signs and tests for identification of impending and current water-loss dehydration in older people. Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2015;CD009647. PMID 25924806 (abstract read on PubMed in this session).
candidates.opening_line_draft: Asking an older person whether they are thirsty tells you less than counting the cups they finished today.
candidates.visual_idea: Checklist card: a row of cup outlines across one day (morning, midday, afternoon, evening) to tick when a cup is finished, with a line saying the daily amount is agreed with the GP or nurse if heart or kidney problems limit fluids. If a number of cups is shown, it carries the label 'Illustrative example'.
candidates.pause: Carers who ask 'are you thirsty?' and always hear 'no'.
candidates.gain: A simple daily measure they can start today, and the reason thirst is not enough.
candidates.follow: Shows the account turns physiology into something a carer can do at home.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E179 (help to drink; offer the cup before a blood test confirms the problem). This differs: it explains why thirst is unreliable and gives a counting method.

candidates.stimulus_use: 'Compare the stated aim of a service with what happens' and 'a service manager' pointed to a ward policy judged by whether it is in place rather than by what patients eat; light switch, weather forecasting, pruning, handovers and three months gave nothing.
candidates.working_title: What protected mealtimes did and did not change
candidates.core_insight: Studies of protected mealtimes found no rise in what patients ate; the approach with better support is hands-on help at the meal.
candidates.angle: The policy's stated aim is more food eaten. A stepped wedge cluster randomised trial and a before-and-after study both measured intake and found no gain. Stopping ward rounds does not by itself open a carton or lift a fork for someone who needs help.
candidates.position: Wards should keep avoidable interruptions away from meals, but judge the policy by whether people who need help receive it and by measured intake, not by whether the policy exists.
claims_needing_evidence: In a stepped wedge cluster randomised trial across three subacute sites in Melbourne (149 participants), energy and protein intake did not differ between protected mealtimes and control periods (Porter 2017).
The trial authors recommend mealtime assistance, food-based approaches and oral nutrition supplements as better-evidenced alternatives (Porter 2017 abstract).

In a London teaching hospital before-and-after study, protected mealtimes did not reduce the proportion of patients interrupted at meals, energy intake did not rise and protein intake fell (Hickson 2011).
Mealtime assistance increases intake in hospital or care home patients (needs a systematic review or trial; see leads).
evidence_leads: Porter J, Haines TP, Truby H. The efficacy of Protected Mealtimes in hospitalised patients: a stepped wedge cluster randomised controlled trial. BMC Med 2017;15:25. PMID 28166787 (abstract read on PubMed in this session).

Hickson M, Connolly A, Whelan K. Impact of protected mealtimes on ward mealtime environment, patient experience and nutrient intake in hospitalised patients. J Hum Nutr Diet 2011;24:370-4. PMID 21585568 (abstract read on PubMed in this session).

Simmons SF et al. Improving food intake in nursing home residents with feeding assistance: a staffing analysis. J Gerontol A 2001;56:M790-4. PMID 11723156 (abstract read on PubMed in this session: half of residents ate more with one-to-one help).
Young AM et al. Improving nutritional care and patient outcomes: comparing assistants' mealtime help with protected mealtimes. Clin Nutr 2013 (unsure).
Howson FFA et al. Can trained volunteers improve the mealtime care of older hospital patients? BMJ Open 2018 (unsure).
candidates.opening_line_draft: Protected mealtimes were meant to help patients eat more. When researchers weighed what people ate, intake did not rise.
candidates.visual_idea: Comparison card. Left column 'What the policy changes': no routine ward rounds, no routine tests, tables cleared. Right column 'What raises intake': someone sitting down to help, packets opened and food cut, supplements offered between meals. Credit line: Porter et al., BMC Med 2017; Hickson et al., J Hum Nutr Diet 2011.
candidates.pause: Nurses and managers who run protected mealtimes and assume they work.
candidates.gain: Trial evidence to redirect effort from the policy to the help.
candidates.follow: Shows the account tests familiar ward practices against measured results.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E108 (nutrition after hip fracture is treatment; feeding is a clinical task). This differs: it evaluates a named ward policy with trial data.

candidates.stimulus_use: 'Take a common shortcut and qualify it' with 'a GP' targeted the BMI shortcut; 'tape measure' and 'scale' suggested mid-upper arm circumference when a person cannot be weighed; weather forecasting, harvesting and the first minute gave nothing.
candidates.working_title: Ask for the weight six months ago before you trust the BMI
candidates.core_insight: A normal BMI can hide malnutrition in an older person; recent unplanned weight loss is the more telling measure, and the GLIM criteria set a higher low-BMI threshold for people aged 70 and over.
candidates.angle: The shortcut 'BMI is fine, so nutrition is fine' misses people who were heavier and are now losing weight. Start with the weight trend. When someone can't stand on scales, a tape measure round the upper arm gives an estimate.
candidates.position: In older people, record a measured weight over time and ask about unplanned loss; a normal BMI is not reassurance on its own.
claims_needing_evidence: MUST scores unplanned weight loss over the past 3 to 6 months (5 to 10% scores 1, more than 10% scores 2) separately from BMI (BAPEN MUST documentation).

GLIM phenotypic criteria include weight loss of more than 5% within 6 months or more than 10% beyond 6 months, low BMI (below 20 under age 70, below 22 at 70 or over, in Western populations) and reduced muscle mass (GLIM consensus, Cederholm 2019).
MUST provides alternative measures, including mid-upper arm circumference, when weight or height can't be measured (BAPEN MUST documentation).
Most primary care studies of weight loss used a clinician's coded symptom rather than a measured weight (Nicholson 2018).
evidence_leads: Cederholm T et al. GLIM criteria for the diagnosis of malnutrition: a consensus report from the global clinical nutrition community. Clin Nutr 2019;38:1-9 (thresholds to confirm in full text).
Elia M (ed.). The 'MUST' report. BAPEN, 2003, and the MUST explanatory booklet (official documents; need an openable copy).

Nicholson BD et al. Weight loss as a predictor of cancer in primary care: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Br J Gen Pract 2018;68:e311-22. PMID 29632004 (abstract read on PubMed in this session: 20 of 25 studies used coded weight loss; one used measured weight).
candidates.opening_line_draft: A normal BMI in an older person tells you little until you know what they weighed six months ago.
candidates.visual_idea: Diagram: a weight timeline with two measured points six months apart and a falling line, beside a normal-range BMI marker. Below, three steps: 'Ask the weight 3 to 6 months ago', 'Then work out BMI (GLIM: low is under 22 at 70 or over)', 'No scales? Measure mid-upper arm circumference'.
candidates.pause: GPs and trainees who use BMI as the whole nutrition check.
candidates.gain: A better first question and one threshold fact to remember.
candidates.follow: Clinical teaching that corrects a routine shortcut with a named standard.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E126 (weight loss, slower walking and needing help with dressing as frailty signs, for families). This differs: a measurement point for clinicians about BMI versus weight trend.

candidates.stimulus_use: 'Compare the stated aim of a service with what happens' with 'averages' led to hospital menus planned around a standard portion, and 'the first 48 hours' to asking early in a stay; recipe card, archives, waiting and GP gave nothing.
candidates.working_title: Is there a menu choice for small appetites?
candidates.core_insight: Hospital menus are planned to meet nutrition standards when a portion is eaten, so a person who eats half of each meal gets roughly half; UK hospital food standards include energy-dense options for people at nutritional risk, and families can ask for them.
candidates.angle: The stated aim is that hospital food meets patients' needs. For an older person with a small appetite, a standard or 'healthier choice' plate eaten by half falls well short. Asking for the options meant for nutritionally vulnerable patients, plus snacks, is a concrete request a relative can make in the first days.
candidates.position: Explanatory, with a practical request: if your relative is eating little in hospital, ask for the energy-dense menu options and snacks between meals, and ask whether a dietitian should see them.
claims_needing_evidence: UK hospital food and catering standards set separate nutrition standards for 'nutritionally well' and 'nutritionally vulnerable' patients, including energy-dense choices and snacks (BDA Nutrition and Hydration Digest; Scottish Food in Hospitals specification; NHS England National Standards for Healthcare Food and Drink 2022).
Older hospital patients on texture-modified diets ate less energy and protein than those on normal diets (Wright 2005).
Subacute inpatients in an Australian trial had a daily energy deficit between intake and estimated requirements (Porter 2017 pilot data cited in abstract).
Menu nutrient analysis assumes the full portion is eaten (needs a catering standards source; otherwise drop this line).
evidence_leads: British Dietetic Association. The Nutrition and Hydration Digest: improving outcomes through food and beverage services (2nd edition or later) (unsure of edition and wording).

Health Facilities Scotland / Scottish Government. Food in Hospitals: National Catering and Nutrition Specification for Food and Fluid Provision in Hospitals in Scotland (2008, revised 2016) (unsure of revision year).
NHS England. National Standards for Healthcare Food and Drink (2022) (official; not openable here).

Wright L et al. Comparison of energy and protein intakes of older people consuming a texture modified diet with a normal hospital diet. J Hum Nutr Diet 2005;18:213-9. PMID 15882384 (abstract read on PubMed in this session).
candidates.opening_line_draft: If your mother is eating half of each hospital meal, ask whether she can have the menu options meant for small appetites.
candidates.visual_idea: Comparison illustration: a standard plate with half left uneaten beside a smaller, energy-dense plate plus two snack items across the day. Labelled 'Illustrative example'; no nutrient numbers unless taken from a named standard.
candidates.pause: Relatives who see half-eaten trays at every visit.
candidates.gain: A specific, reasonable request to make on the ward.
candidates.follow: Practical help for families dealing with hospital routines.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E108 (protein left on the tray after hip fracture) and E180 (a fall in eating as a sign to assess). This differs: it gives families the menu mechanism and a request.

candidates.stimulus_use: 'Change the viewpoint to someone else in the scene' with 'a spouse of 50 years', 'handing over' and 'habit' moved the viewpoint to the person who has shared meals for decades; 'recipe card' suggested a written list of how the person eats; house removals and the first hour gave nothing.
candidates.working_title: Tell the ward how they eat, not only what they like
candidates.core_insight: The spouse or family member who has shared meals with an older person for years knows the details that make eating possible, and good wards ask for this knowledge and welcome carers at mealtimes if both wish.
candidates.angle: Admission paperwork asks about allergies and likes. The partner knows which cup can be held, whether food needs cutting, how slowly the person eats, whether the dentures fit and whether they eat better with company. That knowledge rarely reaches the ward unless someone writes it down.
candidates.position: Hospitals and care homes should ask family carers how the person eats and invite them to mealtimes if both wish; families should offer this knowledge without being expected to supply the ward's mealtime help.
claims_needing_evidence: Person-centred information tools used in UK hospitals, such as Alzheimer's Society 'This is me', include food and drink preferences and needs (official leaflet; check current edition).
John's Campaign supports family carers staying with people with dementia in hospital, including at mealtimes (campaign materials; check wording).
Being dependent on others for feeding was the strongest predictor of aspiration pneumonia in a prospective study, which supports recording how someone eats (Langmore 1998; optional).
Family presence or help at hospital mealtimes is linked with better intake (needs a study; drop if none found).
evidence_leads: Alzheimer's Society. This is me (leaflet, current edition) (unsure of section wording).
John's Campaign, johnscampaign.org.uk (unsure what it states about mealtimes).
Langmore SE et al. Predictors of aspiration pneumonia: how important is dysphagia? Dysphagia 1998;13:69-81. PMID 9513300 (abstract read on PubMed in this session).
candidates.opening_line_draft: Whoever has shared meals with your father for years knows which cup he can hold, how slowly he eats and whether his dentures fit.
candidates.visual_idea: Checklist card titled 'How he eats', with six prompts to fill in and hand to the ward: cup or glass; cutlery or finger food; food cut and packets opened; dentures and glasses in; pace and best time of day; eats better with company. A drawn illustration of an older couple at a table sits beside it.
candidates.pause: Spouses and family carers who feel their knowledge is not asked for.
candidates.gain: A short list to hand over on admission.
candidates.follow: Respects carers as experts in the person, a recurring theme of the account.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E149 (one-page baseline taped above the bed) and E151 (ask the named nurse whether they have eaten). This differs: an eating-specific handover and an invitation to mealtimes.

candidates.stimulus_use: 'Look at the smallest practical detail' with 'a hospital doctor in training' and 'the first minute' led to watching the first minutes of one meal; stopwatch and timing suggested how long eating takes; museum curation and mapping gave nothing.
candidates.working_title: Watch one meal before you write 'eating and drinking well'
candidates.core_insight: A few minutes of watching an older patient eat shows problems that notes and food charts miss: a tray out of reach, sealed packets, slow chewing, coughing, a wet voice, food held in the cheek, tiring halfway.
candidates.angle: For doctors in training whose ward rounds fall between meals: go back at lunchtime once, and know what to look for. The qualification: no cough does not mean no aspiration, so concerns go to speech and language therapy.
candidates.position: Doctors in training should watch at least part of a meal for patients with weight loss, chest infections or suspected swallowing difficulty. This is a practice judgement, supported by evidence that feeding dependency predicts aspiration pneumonia.
claims_needing_evidence: Signs that suggest swallowing difficulty include coughing or choking with food or drink, a wet voice after swallowing, food left in the mouth, prolonged chewing and recurrent chest infections (RCSLT or national stroke guidance; clinical review).
Some people aspirate without coughing (silent aspiration), so bedside observation can't exclude aspiration (review; see leads).
Dependence on others for feeding was the strongest predictor of aspiration pneumonia in older veterans (Langmore 1998).
In usual nursing home care, residents received about 9 minutes of help per meal, compared with 38 minutes needed for one-to-one assistance (Simmons 2001; optional).
evidence_leads: Langmore SE et al. Dysphagia 1998;13:69-81. PMID 9513300 (abstract read on PubMed in this session).
Ramsey DJ, Smithard DG, Kalra L. Silent aspiration: what do we know? Dysphagia 2005;20:218-25 (unsure; not found in this session's searches).
Simmons SF et al. J Gerontol A 2001;56:M790-4. PMID 11723156 (abstract read on PubMed in this session).
Royal College of Speech and Language Therapists, dysphagia clinical guidance (unsure which document).
candidates.opening_line_draft: Go to one lunchtime on your ward and watch how your patients eat.
candidates.visual_idea: Annotated scene: a drawn bedside meal with numbered labels: tray out of reach; sealed pots; cutlery the person can't grip; slumped in bed rather than sitting up; glasses and dentures in the locker; cough or wet voice; food held in the cheek; tiring halfway. A footer line: 'No cough does not rule out aspiration. Refer if in doubt.'
candidates.pause: Trainees who realise they have rarely seen their patients eat.
candidates.gain: An observation list they can use at the next meal.
candidates.follow: Bedside teaching of a kind trainees rarely get.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E187 (a drowsy person with a new wet voice needs assessment of swallow, chest and arousal) and E180 (the tray as a sign). This differs: meal observation as a routine clinical skill.

candidates.stimulus_use: 'Change the viewpoint to someone else in the scene' gave the speech and language therapist's view that a recommendation is made on one day in one illness; 'reversibility' and 'the first 48 hours' framed it as a snapshot that needs a review; tide table, archives and timing gave nothing extra.
candidates.working_title: When will the swallow be checked again?
candidates.core_insight: Thickened drinks or soft food recommended during an acute illness are a snapshot; many swallowing problems improve, so each recommendation needs a review date and a named person to review it.
candidates.angle: From the therapist's side, the recommendation fitted the person on the day of assessment. Families can ask when it will be reviewed, especially before a move to a care home, because thickened drinks have costs: people tend to drink less and enjoy it less.
candidates.position: Every modified food or drink recommendation should state when and by whom it will be reviewed; families are right to ask.
claims_needing_evidence: After a first stroke, about half of patients had a clinically detected swallowing abnormality at presentation, and 87% of survivors had returned to their usual diet by 6 months (Mann 1999; stroke population).

In people with dementia or Parkinson's who aspirated thin liquids, those assigned thickened liquids had more dehydration than those assigned a chin-down posture (6% vs 2%), with no clear difference in pneumonia (Robbins 2008 RCT).
IDDSI levels describe standard drink thicknesses and food textures used in UK practice (Cichero 2017).
Swallowing often improves as an acute illness other than stroke resolves (needs a source; otherwise keep the post to the review principle).
evidence_leads: Mann G, Hankey GJ, Cameron D. Swallowing function after stroke: prognosis and prognostic factors at 6 months. Stroke 1999;30:744-8. PMID 10187872 (abstract read on PubMed in this session).

Robbins J et al. Comparison of 2 interventions for liquid aspiration on pneumonia incidence: a randomized trial. Ann Intern Med 2008;148:509-18. PMID 18378947 (abstract read on PubMed in this session).

Cichero JAY et al. Development of international terminology and definitions for texture-modified foods and thickened fluids used in dysphagia management: the IDDSI framework. Dysphagia 2017;32:293-314. PMID 27913916 (abstract read on PubMed in this session).
RCSLT guidance on reviewing dysphagia recommendations (unsure).
candidates.opening_line_draft: Thickened drinks started during an illness should come with a date for the next swallow check. Ask for that date.
candidates.visual_idea: Timeline diagram: illness begins; swallow assessed (date); recommendation made; review date; at review the options 'continue', 'change' or 'stop'. A stamp-style label on the recommendation reads 'Review by: ___'.
candidates.pause: Families whose relative has been on thickened drinks for months with no one mentioning a review.
candidates.gain: One question to ask and the reason it is fair.
candidates.follow: Helps families take part in decisions that are often made without them.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E187 (do not thicken the diet and miss the pneumonia). This differs: review and reversibility of swallowing recommendations, for families.

candidates.stimulus_use: 'Look at the smallest practical detail' with 'timing', 'a hospital doctor in training' and 'the first hour' led to the dose times of Parkinson's medicines when a patient is made nil by mouth; library card, weather forecasting and signposting gave nothing.
candidates.working_title: Nil by mouth still needs a plan for Parkinson's medicines
candidates.core_insight: When a person with Parkinson's can't swallow safely, their dopaminergic medicines still need to be given on time by another route, and that plan belongs in the same moment the nil by mouth order is written.
candidates.angle: A small detail for doctors in training: when you write nil by mouth for someone with Parkinson's, prescribe the alternative (via a nasogastric tube if one is in place, or a skin patch using a recognised conversion method) and match the dose times to the person's home schedule. In one UK hospital, 39% of scheduled levodopa doses were omitted or given more than 30 minutes late.
candidates.position: Doctors who write nil by mouth for a person with Parkinson's should arrange an alternative route for their medicines at the same time and seek specialist advice if unsure. The post must also state that the Derby study found no link between late doses and length of stay.
claims_needing_evidence: In 737 emergency admissions of people with Parkinson's at one UK hospital, 39% of scheduled levodopa doses were omitted or given more than 30 minutes late; delays were not associated with length of stay (Skelly 2017).

Guidance recommends continuing dopaminergic medicines around surgery or when the oral route is lost, using alternative routes such as a nasogastric tube or transdermal rotigotine (Brennan and Genever 2010; NICE NG71).
Abrupt withdrawal of dopaminergic medicines can cause serious complications, including a rare parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia syndrome (needs a review or guideline source).
Swallowing in Parkinson's can worsen when medicines wear off (needs a source; drop if not found).
evidence_leads: Skelly R, Brown L, Fogarty A. Delayed administration of dopaminergic drugs is not associated with prolonged length of stay of hospitalized patients with Parkinson's disease. Parkinsonism Relat Disord 2017;35:25-29. PMID 27889470 (abstract read on PubMed in this session).
Brennan KA, Genever RW. Managing Parkinson's disease during surgery. BMJ 2010;341:c5718. PMID 21041319 (no abstract; full text needed).
NICE NG71. Parkinson's disease in adults (2017) (official; not openable here).
Parkinson's UK 'Get It On Time' materials and the OPTIMAL medication calculator (unsure of current versions).
candidates.opening_line_draft: When you write 'nil by mouth' for someone with Parkinson's, write the plan for their levodopa in the same minute.
candidates.visual_idea: Flow diagram: 'Swallow unsafe or nil by mouth' leads to 'Keep dopaminergic medicines going', which branches to 'Nasogastric tube in place: give via tube as advised by pharmacy' and 'No tube: patch using a conversion method; ask pharmacy or the Parkinson's team', then 'Match home dose times' and 'Review every day'. No doses shown.
candidates.pause: Junior doctors who have met this problem at night or at a weekend.
candidates.gain: A sequence to follow the next time they write nil by mouth.
candidates.follow: Precise, safety-focused teaching that also states an inconvenient finding.
candidates.earlier_overlap: none

candidates.stimulus_use: 'Count something nobody counts' with 'packing' (read as packaging) and 'visibility' led to counting sealed packets returned on a tray; 'a spouse of 50 years' nudged the role of visitors in opening them; envelope, football refereeing and the first hour gave nothing.
candidates.working_title: Count the sealed packets on the tray
candidates.core_insight: Many older people can't open the cheese portions, cartons and foil-sealed pots served in hospitals, so food that arrives and leaves unopened was never available to eat.
candidates.angle: Count the unopened packets on returned trays. In one study of well older people, around 4 in 10 could not open a cheese portion, and opening was harder lying in bed than sitting in a chair.
candidates.position: Staff and visitors should open packets and help people sit up to eat; food returned unopened should be recorded as not accessible, not as refused.
claims_needing_evidence: Of 40 well community-dwelling people over 65 tested on hospital packaging, 39% could not open cheese portions and 10% could not open water bottles; tetra packs, cereals, fruit cups and desserts were among the hardest (Bell 2016, Appetite).
Earlier research with hospitalised people over 65 in New South Wales found difficulty opening milk, water, juices, cereal and tetra packs (cited in Bell 2016 abstract; original study to check).

Pinch strength and dexterity were worse when opening packs in a hospital bed than in a chair, and 15% of cheese portions could not be opened in either position (Bell 2017, J Hum Nutr Diet; 34 participants).
These studies were done in Australia with well older people; packaging in UK hospitals may differ (state as a limitation).
evidence_leads: Bell AF, Walton KL, Tapsell LC. Easy to open? Exploring the 'openability' of hospital food and beverage packaging by older adults. Appetite 2016;98:125-32. PMID 26686584 (abstract read on PubMed in this session).

Bell A, Tapsell L, Walton K, Yoxall A. Accessing hospital packaged foods and beverages: the importance of a seated posture when eating. J Hum Nutr Diet 2017;30:394-402. PMID 27731524 (abstract read on PubMed in this session).
Bell AF et al. Accessing packaged food and beverages in hospital: exploring experiences of patients and staff. Appetite 2013 (unsure).
candidates.opening_line_draft: About 4 in 10 well older people in one study could not open a hospital cheese portion [verify: 39%, Bell 2016].
candidates.visual_idea: Annotated scene: a hospital tray seen from above with a sealed cheese portion, butter portion, juice carton, foil-lidded pudding and wrapped sandwich, each labelled 'hard to open'. A small inset compares opening a pack while lying in bed and while sitting in a chair. Credit line: Bell et al., Appetite 2016; J Hum Nutr Diet 2017.
candidates.pause: A tray every visitor and nurse will recognise.
candidates.gain: Two actions: open the packets, and help the person sit up to eat.
candidates.follow: The account notices small, fixable details that change care.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E180 (a fall in eating as a sign) and E108 (protein left on the tray). This differs: a specific, measured barrier to eating and what to do about it.

candidates.stimulus_use: 'Test a familiar slogan against the evidence' took the belief that older people need less food; 'a physiotherapist' and 'the moment of discharge' pointed to rebuilding muscle after illness; kitchen sieve, weather forecasting, handing over and rhythm gave nothing.
candidates.working_title: Fewer calories, not less protein
candidates.core_insight: Older people often need fewer calories than when they were younger, but expert groups recommend the same or more protein per kilogram of body weight, and more during and after illness.
candidates.angle: The belief 'you need less food as you get older' is half true and leads to small, low-protein meals. The calorie half holds for many; the protein half does not, and recovery after a hospital stay needs protein, energy and activity together.
candidates.position: Older people, especially when recovering from illness, should keep protein intake up even when appetite is smaller; people with severe kidney disease need individual advice.
claims_needing_evidence: The PROT-AGE group recommends at least 1.0 to 1.2 g of protein per kg body weight per day for people over 65, and 1.2 to 1.5 g/kg for most older people with acute or chronic disease, with an exception for severe kidney disease not on dialysis (Bauer 2013).
The UK reference nutrient intake for protein in adults is about 0.75 g per kg per day (COMA 1991; to verify).
Energy requirements tend to fall with age, mainly through lower physical activity and lean mass (SACN energy report 2011; to verify).
ESPEN recommends about 1 g protein per kg per day for older people, adjusted for illness (ESPEN geriatrics guideline 2019; full text needed).
evidence_leads: Bauer J et al. Evidence-based recommendations for optimal dietary protein intake in older people: a position paper from the PROT-AGE Study Group. J Am Med Dir Assoc 2013;14:542-59. PMID 23867520 (abstract read on PubMed in this session).
Volkert D et al. ESPEN guideline on clinical nutrition and hydration in geriatrics. Clin Nutr 2019;38:10-47 (protein figure to confirm).
Scientific Advisory Committee on Nutrition. Dietary Reference Values for Energy (2011) (official; unsure of openable copy).
Department of Health. Dietary Reference Values for Food Energy and Nutrients for the United Kingdom (COMA report 41, 1991) (unsure of openable copy).
candidates.opening_line_draft: Many people believe older people need less food. Most need fewer calories and at least as much protein.
candidates.visual_idea: Comparison card with two columns: 'Calories: often fewer than at 40' and 'Protein: the same or more per kg, and more after illness'. Beneath, drawn everyday protein foods (eggs, milk, yoghurt, cheese, beans, fish) with a note: 'Kidney disease? Ask for individual advice.'
candidates.pause: Families who have been shrinking portions for a parent.
candidates.gain: A clear distinction and familiar foods to act on.
candidates.follow: Tests common beliefs against expert recommendations.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E108 (nutrition after hip fracture). This differs: a general principle about protein and calories for the public.

candidates.stimulus_use: 'Compare what is recorded with what is experienced' with 'the last week of life' set a fluid chart in millilitres against a dying person's dry mouth; thermostat, bakeries, returning, habit and physiotherapist gave nothing.
candidates.working_title: Near the end of life, a dry mouth is eased at the mouth
candidates.core_insight: Near death, thirst and a dry mouth are usually eased by frequent mouth care and small sips, while fluids by drip or under the skin are a separate decision whose effect on comfort is uncertain.
candidates.angle: The chart records millilitres; the person experiences a dry mouth. Studies of people near death found thirst and dry mouth were relieved by mouth care and sips far smaller than the amounts that prevent dehydration. Families can do this care themselves if they want to.
candidates.position: Frequent mouth care should be a standard part of care in the last days of life. Clinically assisted hydration should be discussed person by person, not given or withheld by default. The evidence comes mainly from people with cancer, which the post should say.
claims_needing_evidence: NICE guidance on care of dying adults advises supporting people to drink if they wish, offering frequent mouth care, and discussing the risks and benefits of clinically assisted hydration (NICE NG31, 2015).

In 32 terminally ill patients in a comfort care unit, hunger and thirst were absent or only initial in most, and in all patients hunger, thirst and dry mouth could be relieved with small amounts of food and fluid, ice chips and lip lubrication (McCann 1994; mostly cancer).
In a hospice RCT of 129 people with advanced cancer, 1 litre a day of parenteral fluid did not improve dehydration symptoms, quality of life or survival compared with 100 mL (Bruera 2013).
Evidence in older people dying from conditions other than cancer is limited (state as a limitation).
evidence_leads: NICE NG31. Care of dying adults in the last days of life (2015) (official; not openable here; seek a published copy).

candidates.opening_line_draft: Near the end of life, thirst and a dry mouth are usually eased by mouth care and small sips, given often.
candidates.visual_idea: Drawn illustration: a family member gently moistening the lips of an older person resting in bed, with a short checklist beside it: offer sips if wanted; moisten the mouth with a soft swab; lip balm; clean teeth or dentures gently; ask the nurse how often and what to use. Warm sand background.
candidates.pause: Families who fear a dying relative is thirsty and feel there is nothing they can do.
candidates.gain: Something useful and kind they can do, and a clearer view of the drip decision.
candidates.follow: Humane, evidence-based care near death, without abandonment or overtreatment.
candidates.earlier_overlap: none

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'find an outcome that patients value and the routine measure misses' produced the whole idea; sewing pattern, air traffic control, stocktaking, habit, physiotherapist and five years gave nothing.
candidates.working_title: Safe to swallow, and still worth eating
candidates.core_insight: People with swallowing problems value enjoying food, eating with others and not feeling afraid at meals, and routine swallowing plans rarely record any of these.
candidates.angle: Swallowing plans record texture levels, drink thickness and chest infections. In a four-country survey, more than a third of people with swallowing problems avoided eating with others and about 4 in 10 felt anxiety or panic at mealtimes.
candidates.position: Swallowing care should record whether the person enjoys meals, eats with others and is eating enough, alongside safety measures; texture-modified food should look and taste like food.
claims_needing_evidence: In 360 people with swallowing problems in nursing homes and clinics in Germany, France, Spain and the UK, 84% felt eating should be enjoyable but 45% found it so; 41% had anxiety or panic at mealtimes; 36% avoided eating with others (Ekberg 2002).
Older inpatients on texture-modified diets ate less energy (3877 vs 6115 kJ a day) and protein (40 vs 60 g) than those on a normal hospital diet (Wright 2005; 55 patients).
Validated questionnaires exist for swallowing-related quality of life (e.g. SWAL-QOL) (instrument paper; check suitability for older people).
evidence_leads: Ekberg O et al. Social and psychological burden of dysphagia: its impact on diagnosis and treatment. Dysphagia 2002;17:139-46. PMID 11956839 (abstract read on PubMed in this session).
Wright L et al. J Hum Nutr Diet 2005;18:213-9. PMID 15882384 (abstract read on PubMed in this session).
McHorney CA et al. The SWAL-QOL and SWAL-CARE outcomes tool for oropharyngeal dysphagia in adults. Dysphagia 2002 (unsure).
Swan K et al. Living with oropharyngeal dysphagia: effects of bolus modification on health-related quality of life, a systematic review. Qual Life Res 2015 (unsure).
candidates.opening_line_draft: More than a third of people with swallowing problems in one European survey avoided eating with other people.
candidates.visual_idea: Comparison card: left 'What the swallowing plan records' (texture level, drink thickness, chest infections); right 'What people told researchers' (fear at meals, eating alone, food that no longer tastes like food). candidates.pause: Therapists, nurses and families who focus on safety and sense something is missing.
candidates.gain: A finding and three questions to add to swallowing reviews.
candidates.follow: Keeps the person's experience in view alongside clinical risk.
candidates.earlier_overlap: none

candidates.stimulus_use: 'Reveal what is omitted' with 'a speech and language therapist' (whose assessment covers food and drink) and 'handing over' pointed to the tablets left out of many swallowing plans; wall calendar, air traffic control, rhythm and the first month gave nothing.
candidates.working_title: The swallowing plan that forgets the tablets
candidates.core_insight: Swallowing assessments set food and drink textures, but tablets are a separate problem: residents with swallowing difficulty had far more medicine administration errors in a UK care home study, and crushing or mixing tablets can change how they work.
candidates.angle: The omitted item is the medicine list. For each tablet: is it still needed, is there a liquid, dispersible or patch form, can it be crushed safely, and who checked?
candidates.position: Whenever a swallowing problem is recorded, a pharmacist or prescriber should review the medicine list, including whether each medicine is still needed.
claims_needing_evidence: In North Yorkshire care homes with nursing (738 observed administrations, 166 residents), medicine administration error rates were 57.3% for residents with dysphagia and 30.8% for those without (Serrano Santos 2016).
Crushing modified-release or enteric-coated tablets can alter drug release and cause harm (pharmacy reference or UK consensus guideline).
Mixing medicines with thickened fluids may change how the drug is released (laboratory study; needs a source).
Residents with dysphagia were more likely to experience inappropriate prescribing in the same study (Serrano Santos 2016).
evidence_leads: Serrano Santos JM, Poland F, Wright D, Longmore T. Medicines administration for residents with dysphagia in care homes: a small scale observational study to improve practice. Int J Pharm 2016;512:416-21. PMID 26906457 (abstract read on PubMed in this session).
Wright D et al. Consensus guideline on the medication management of adults with swallowing difficulties (UK) (unsure of year and publisher).
Kelly J, Wright D, Wood J. Medicine administration errors in patients with dysphagia in secondary care: a multi-centre observational study. J Adv Nurs 2011 (unsure; citation lookup was ambiguous).
Manrique-Torres YJ et al. The effect of thickening agents on drug dissolution (2014) (unsure).
candidates.opening_line_draft: A swallowing assessment sets the texture of food and drink. Someone still has to decide what happens to the tablets.
candidates.visual_idea: Checklist card titled 'For each tablet': still needed? another form (liquid, dispersible, patch)? safe to crush? who checked, and when? A drawn pill organiser beside a cup of thickened drink.
candidates.pause: Nurses and pharmacists who have seen tablets crushed into yoghurt without a plan.
candidates.gain: Four questions that turn a swallowing plan into a medicines review.
candidates.follow: Joins swallowing care and medicines safety, which are often handled separately.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E135 to E148 (medicines posts on anticholinergics, sedatives and delirium risk). This differs: medicine form and administration in people with swallowing difficulty.

candidates.stimulus_use: 'Test a familiar slogan against the evidence' took 'mouth care prevents pneumonia'; 'order of events' suggested that a programme can only reduce pneumonia after it improves oral hygiene and keeps it up; shopping list, football refereeing, rerouting, ward clerk and five years gave nothing.
candidates.working_title: Mouth care and pneumonia: less certain than the slogan
candidates.core_insight: Trials of care home mouth care programmes have not shown a clear fall in pneumonia, so the firmer reasons to clean an older person's mouth are comfort, eating, finding sore spots and dignity.
candidates.angle: The slogan 'mouth care prevents pneumonia' is widely taught. A cluster randomised trial in 14 US nursing homes found no significant reduction over two years, and a 2022 Cochrane review found the effect on pneumonia unclear. Mouth care is justified without that claim.
candidates.position: Mouth care should be done for its direct benefits; claims that it prevents pneumonia should be described as uncertain, not as established.
claims_needing_evidence: In a cluster randomised trial of 2152 residents in 14 US nursing homes, the Mouth Care Without a Battle programme did not significantly reduce pneumonia over two years (0.67 vs 0.72 per 1000 resident-days); a post hoc first-year analysis found a reduction (Zimmerman 2020).

A 2022 Cochrane review (6 RCTs, 6244 participants, all high risk of bias) found insufficient evidence of a difference between professional and usual oral care in pneumonia incidence, with low-certainty evidence of fewer pneumonia deaths at 24 months (Cao 2022).
No trials compared oral care with no oral care (Cao 2022).
Earlier Japanese nursing home trials reported fewer pneumonias with professional oral care (Yoneyama; to check).
evidence_leads: Zimmerman S et al. Effectiveness of a mouth care program provided by nursing home staff vs standard care on reducing pneumonia incidence: a cluster randomized trial. JAMA Netw Open 2020;3:e204321. PMID 32558913 (abstract read on PubMed in this session).
Cao Y et al. Oral care measures for preventing nursing home-acquired pneumonia. Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2022;CD012416.pub3. PMID 36383760 (abstract read on PubMed in this session).
Yoneyama T et al. Oral care reduces pneumonia in older patients in nursing homes. J Am Geriatr Soc 2002;50:430-3 (unsure).
candidates.opening_line_draft: A mouth care programme tested in 14 US nursing homes, with over 2,000 residents, did not show a clear fall in pneumonia over two years.
candidates.visual_idea: Comparison card: 'What trials show about pneumonia: uncertain' (trial and Cochrane credit lines) beside 'What mouth care does anyway': a clean, comfortable mouth; easier eating and denture wearing; sore spots and broken teeth found early. Credit: Zimmerman et al., JAMA Netw Open 2020; Cao et al., Cochrane 2022.
candidates.pause: Clinicians and educators who repeat the pneumonia claim in training.
candidates.gain: An accurate summary of the trials and a sturdier reason for mouth care.
candidates.follow: Willing to question a claim the account's readers support.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E051 (mouth on the checklist before labelling distress). This differs: the evidence on mouth care and pneumonia.

candidates.stimulus_use: The same slogan-testing operation applied to 'when in doubt, keep them nil by mouth'; 'order of events' pointed to the timing of first oral intake and 'rerouting' to alternative routes for fluids and medicines.
candidates.working_title: Nil by mouth is a treatment with side effects
candidates.core_insight: Keeping an older person with aspiration pneumonia nil by mouth 'to be safe' was linked in one cohort with poorer intake, longer treatment and loss of swallowing ability, so the order needs a reason, a review time and prompt swallow assessment.
candidates.angle: The reflex order on admission is written as if it has no cost. In a Japanese cohort, tentative nil by mouth was associated with a longer treatment course and greater decline in swallowing than early oral intake. The finding is observational, but it shifts the question from 'is eating safe?' to 'what does waiting cost?'.
candidates.position: Nil by mouth orders for older people should state the reason, the time of review and the plan for fluids, medicines and mouth care, with swallow assessment arranged promptly.
claims_needing_evidence: In a retrospective cohort of 331 patients with aspiration pneumonia who ate normally before admission, tentative nil by mouth was associated with poorer nutritional intake in the first week, a longer treatment duration (median 13 vs 8 days) and greater decline in swallowing ability, after inverse probability weighting (Maeda 2016).
The design is observational and may be confounded by illness severity (state in the post).
Early oral intake after aspiration pneumonia was associated with better function in another cohort (Koyama 2015; to check).
evidence_leads: Maeda K, Koga T, Akagi J. Tentative nil per os leads to poor outcomes in older adults with aspiration pneumonia. Clin Nutr 2016;35:1147-52. PMID 26481947 (abstract read on PubMed in this session).

Koyama T et al. Early commencement of oral intake and physical function after onset of aspiration pneumonia: propensity score matching analysis. J Am Geriatr Soc 2015 (unsure; not found in this session's search).
candidates.opening_line_draft: Writing 'nil by mouth' on admission for aspiration pneumonia was linked, in a Japanese study, with longer treatment and worse swallowing.
candidates.visual_idea: Comparison card: 'Nil by mouth, as often written' (two words) beside 'Nil by mouth, complete order': reason; review time; fluids; medicines route; mouth care; who assesses the swallow and when.
candidates.pause: Admitting doctors who write the order by reflex.
candidates.gain: A fuller order they can write the same night.
candidates.follow: Weighs a routine safety measure against its costs.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E187 (do not thicken the diet and miss the pneumonia). This differs: the costs and completeness of a nil by mouth order.

candidates.working_title: Aspiration pneumonia needs more than a weak swallow
candidates.core_insight: In a prospective study of older veterans, needing help to eat and needing help with mouth care predicted aspiration pneumonia better than a swallowing problem alone.
candidates.angle: Aspiration pneumonia is often treated as a swallowing problem to be solved with thicker drinks. The study's authors concluded that dysphagia is an important risk but generally not enough on its own; what is swallowed (saliva from a dirty mouth) and who is helping the person eat also count.
candidates.position: Preventing aspiration pneumonia should include teeth and mouth care and attentive help with eating, not only texture changes.
claims_needing_evidence: In 189 older people (VA Ann Arbor outpatients, acute wards and nursing home) followed for up to 4 years, the best predictors of aspiration pneumonia included dependence for feeding, dependence for oral care, number of decayed teeth, tube feeding, more than one diagnosis, number of medicines and smoking (Langmore 1998).
The authors concluded dysphagia was an important risk but generally not sufficient to cause pneumonia unless other risk factors were present (Langmore 1998 abstract).
The population was US veterans, mostly men (state as a limitation); do not convert the reported odds ratio into 'times more likely'.
evidence_leads: Langmore SE et al. Predictors of aspiration pneumonia: how important is dysphagia? Dysphagia 1998;13:69-81. PMID 9513300 (abstract read on PubMed in this session).
Langmore SE et al. Predictors of aspiration pneumonia in nursing home residents. Dysphagia 2002;17:298-307 (unsure).
candidates.opening_line_draft: Needing help to eat, and needing help to clean the mouth, predicted aspiration pneumonia in older veterans better than a swallowing problem alone.
candidates.visual_idea: Teaching diagram of three overlapping circles labelled 'Something goes the wrong way (swallow)', 'What goes down carries bacteria (mouth and teeth)' and 'The body can't clear it (dependency, illness)', with pneumonia in the overlap. Labelled 'Teaching model based on Langmore et al., 1998'.
candidates.pause: Clinicians who equate aspiration pneumonia with a failed swallow test.
candidates.gain: A wider prevention list: teeth, mouth care, help with eating.
candidates.follow: Teaching that changes how a common diagnosis is understood.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E187 (aspiration and delirium; do not thicken and miss the pneumonia). This differs: risk factors beyond the swallow itself.

candidates.working_title: Nothing by mouth, and still a mouth to clean
candidates.core_insight: People fed by tube still need their teeth and mouth cleaned every day; in one study, tube-fed older people carried potentially harmful bacteria in the throat far more often than those who ate by mouth.
candidates.angle: It is easy to assume a mouth that takes no food needs little care. Eating and drinking help keep the mouth clean, and a tube-fed person loses that. The study is an association, but it points to a simple daily task.
candidates.position: Daily mouth care should be written into every care plan for people who are tube-fed or nil by mouth.
claims_needing_evidence: In 215 patients in six Israeli nursing and skilled nursing facilities, potentially pathogenic bacteria were found in the throat in 81% of nasogastric-fed, 51% of gastrostomy-fed and 17.5% of orally fed patients (Leibovitz 2003).
Pseudomonas aeruginosa was cultured in 31% of nasogastric-fed and none of the orally fed group (Leibovitz 2003).
UK guidance recommends daily support with mouth care for care home residents (NICE NG48, 2016).
Tube feeding was among the predictors of aspiration pneumonia in Langmore 1998 (optional).
evidence_leads: Leibovitz A et al. Pathogenic colonization of oral flora in frail elderly patients fed by nasogastric tube or percutaneous enterogastric tube. J Gerontol A 2003;58:M52-5. PMID 12560411 (abstract read on PubMed in this session).
NICE NG48. Oral health for adults in care homes (2016) (official; not openable here).
Langmore SE et al. Dysphagia 1998. PMID 9513300 (abstract read on PubMed in this session).
candidates.opening_line_draft: A person fed through a tube eats nothing by mouth. Their teeth and gums still need cleaning every day.
candidates.visual_idea: Drawn illustration: a care worker, sitting at eye level, gently brushing the teeth of an older man who is sitting up with a nasogastric tube in place. Beside it: 'Sit up. Small soft brush. Moist swab for gums and tongue. Lip balm.'
candidates.pause: Families and staff who assumed a tube-fed mouth needs little attention.
candidates.gain: A daily task with a clear reason.
candidates.follow: Practical detail that families can check for.
candidates.earlier_overlap: none

candidates.working_title: Feeding tubes in advanced dementia: what the evidence shows
candidates.core_insight: For people with advanced dementia who are eating less, studies have not shown that feeding tubes help them live longer or more comfortably, and careful hand feeding is the recommended approach.
candidates.angle: Declining a tube is a decision about one treatment's likely benefit and harms; it does not mean stopping food, drink or care. Careful hand feeding continues, guided by what the person wanted.
candidates.position: For people with advanced dementia, careful hand feeding should be offered and tube feeding should not be routine. This is a judgement about the treatment, never about the person's worth.
claims_needing_evidence: A 2021 Cochrane review found no randomised trials and 14 non-randomised studies; there was no evidence that tube feeding improves survival or quality of life, PEG feeding was linked with a higher risk of pressure ulcers (moderate certainty), and the balance of evidence suggested more pneumonia with tube feeding (Davies 2021).

The American Geriatrics Society does not recommend feeding tubes in advanced dementia, states that careful hand feeding is as good for death, aspiration pneumonia, function and comfort, and links tube feeding with agitation, restraint and new pressure ulcers (AGS 2014).
NICE advises against routine enteral feeding in people with severe dementia unless indicated for a potentially reversible condition (NICE NG97, 2018; wording to confirm).
evidence_leads: Davies N et al. Enteral tube feeding for people with severe dementia. Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2021;CD013503.pub2. PMID 34387363 (abstract read on PubMed in this session).
American Geriatrics Society feeding tubes in advanced dementia position statement. J Am Geriatr Soc 2014;62:1590-3. PMID 25039796 (abstract read on PubMed in this session).
NICE NG97. Dementia: assessment, management and support for people living with dementia and their carers (2018) (official; recommendation number unsure).
Palecek EJ et al. Comfort feeding only: a proposal to bring clarity to decision-making regarding difficulty with eating for persons with advanced dementia. J Am Geriatr Soc 2010 (unsure).
candidates.opening_line_draft: When a person with advanced dementia eats less, a feeding tube can seem the caring choice. Studies have not shown that it helps people live longer or more comfortably.
candidates.visual_idea: Comparison card: 'Tube feeding: what studies found' (no clear gain in survival or comfort; more pressure ulcers with PEG in a large study) beside 'Careful hand feeding: what it involves' (sitting upright, small mouthfuls, favourite foods, time, stopping when the person signals). Credit: Davies et al., Cochrane 2021; AGS 2014.
candidates.pause: Families facing the question and practitioners who are asked to 'do something'.
candidates.gain: A clear summary and a description of the alternative that is care, not withdrawal.
candidates.follow: Handles hard decisions with evidence and without abandonment.
candidates.earlier_overlap: none

candidates.working_title: Eating and drinking with acknowledged risks: doing it well
candidates.core_insight: When a person chooses to keep eating food that carries a swallowing risk, or when thickened drinks no longer fit their goals, a documented shared decision with practical risk reduction respects their choice and keeps care going.
candidates.angle: UK speech and language therapy guidance frames this as a multidisciplinary shared decision with capacity assessment where needed, clear documentation and continued support, not as the team stepping back.
candidates.position: Decisions to eat and drink with acknowledged risks should be planned with the person and family, recorded, supported with practical measures and reviewed.
claims_needing_evidence: The Royal College of Speech and Language Therapists published multidisciplinary guidance on eating and drinking with acknowledged risks in 2021 (official document; check title and content).
The Royal College of Physicians published guidance on supporting people who have eating and drinking difficulties (2021 update) (official document; check).
Adults with capacity can decline recommended modified textures (Mental Capacity Act 2005; Adults with Incapacity (Scotland) Act 2000).
Thickened liquids were linked with more dehydration than a chin-down posture in a randomised trial (Robbins 2008).
evidence_leads: Royal College of Speech and Language Therapists. Eating and drinking with acknowledged risks: multidisciplinary team guidance for the shared decision-making process (adults), 2021 (unsure of openable copy).

Royal College of Physicians. Supporting people who have eating and drinking difficulties: a guide to practical care and clinical assistance, particularly towards the end of life (2021 update) (unsure).
Robbins J et al. Ann Intern Med 2008;148:509-18. PMID 18378947 (abstract read on PubMed in this session).
candidates.opening_line_draft: A person with capacity may choose ordinary food despite a swallowing risk. The team's work continues: agree the plan, reduce the risk, record it, review it.
candidates.visual_idea: Flow diagram: concern raised; capacity and goals discussed; options and risks explained in plain words; shared decision recorded; risk reduction (sitting upright, supervision, mouth care, chosen textures); review date.
candidates.pause: Teams unsure what their role is once a patient declines modified textures.
candidates.gain: A sequence that respects choice and keeps support in place.
candidates.follow: Combines respect for agency with careful clinical practice.
candidates.earlier_overlap: none

candidates.working_title: Dry mouth and dark urine are poor tests for dehydration in older people
candidates.core_insight: A Cochrane review found that common bedside signs, including urine colour, a dry mouth and feeling thirsty, should not be relied on alone to detect dehydration in older people; serum osmolality is the reference test.
candidates.angle: The shortcut of judging hydration from urine colour or a dry tongue misleads in both directions. Measure or calculate serum osmolality when it counts, and watch drinking behaviour: missing drinks between meals was one of the few signs with some signal.
candidates.position: Don't diagnose or exclude water-loss dehydration in older people from single bedside signs; use serum osmolality when the answer affects care.
claims_needing_evidence: Across 24 studies in people aged 65 and over, tests including fluid intake, urine specific gravity, urine colour, urine volume, heart rate, dry mouth and feeling thirsty were not useful on their own for detecting water-loss dehydration (Hooper 2015 Cochrane).
Missing drinks between meals and expressing fatigue showed some diagnostic ability in one study of 71 people (Hooper 2015).
The reference standard used was serum osmolality, with 295 mOsm/kg or more counted as impending or current dehydration and over 300 as current (Hooper 2015).
In UK care homes, thirst was not associated with hydration status (Hooper 2016 DRIE).
evidence_leads: Hooper L et al. Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2015;CD009647. PMID 25924806 (abstract read on PubMed in this session).
Hooper L et al. J Gerontol A 2016;71:1341-7. PMID 26553658 (abstract read on PubMed in this session).
A validated calculated osmolarity equation for older people (Hooper or Siervo, around 2015) (unsure).
candidates.opening_line_draft: Urine colour, a dry mouth and feeling thirsty all failed as single tests for dehydration in older people in a Cochrane review.
candidates.visual_idea: Comparison card: 'Stop relying on these alone' (urine colour, dry mouth, thirst, heart rate) beside 'What helps' (serum osmolality, measured or calculated; noticing missed drinks between meals). Credit: Hooper et al., Cochrane 2015.
candidates.pause: Clinicians who use urine colour charts or tongue checks every day.
candidates.gain: A corrected habit and the test to use instead.
candidates.follow: Teaching that questions bedside habits with systematic evidence.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E179 (offer the cup; the empty jug shows the problem before a blood test). This differs: diagnostic accuracy of signs, for practitioners.

candidates.working_title: Five days of eating little changes how feeding should start
candidates.core_insight: An older person who has eaten little or nothing for more than five days is at risk of refeeding problems, so NICE advises starting nutrition support cautiously and checking for higher-risk features.
candidates.angle: Refeeding syndrome is taught with examples from eating disorders. The common geriatric case is the person admitted after days of poor intake at home or with weeks of weight loss, then started on full supplements or feeds.
candidates.position: Before starting full feeds or supplements in older people with poor recent intake, screen for refeeding risk and follow NICE CG32.
claims_needing_evidence: NICE CG32 advises that people who have eaten little or nothing for more than 5 days should have nutrition support introduced at no more than 50% of requirements for the first 2 days (official guideline; wording to confirm).

NICE CG32 high-risk criteria include one of: BMI under 16, unintentional weight loss over 15% in 3 to 6 months, little or no intake for over 10 days, or low potassium, phosphate or magnesium before feeding; or two of: BMI under 18.5, weight loss over 10%, little intake for over 5 days, alcohol misuse or certain drugs (official guideline; confirm).
For high-risk patients, NICE advises a low starting rate, thiamine and vitamin B supplementation, and monitoring of electrolytes (official guideline; confirm).
Refeeding syndrome involves shifts in phosphate, potassium and magnesium when feeding restarts (clinical review).
evidence_leads: NICE CG32. Nutrition support for adults: oral nutrition support, enteral tube feeding and parenteral nutrition (2006, updated 2017) (official; not openable here; seek a published copy).
Mehanna HM, Moledina J, Travis J. Refeeding syndrome: what it is, and how to prevent and treat it. BMJ 2008;336:1495-8 (unsure of pages).
da Silva JSV et al. ASPEN consensus recommendations for refeeding syndrome. Nutr Clin Pract 2020 (unsure).
candidates.opening_line_draft: If an older person has eaten little or nothing for more than five days, NICE advises starting nutrition support at no more than half of their needs for the first two days [verify wording in CG32].
candidates.visual_idea: Flow card: 'Eaten little for more than 5 days?' leads to 'Start at no more than half of needs for 2 days', then 'Check high-risk criteria', then for high risk 'Lower start, thiamine, daily potassium, phosphate and magnesium'. Footer: 'Follow your local protocol.'
candidates.pause: Doctors and dietitians who prescribe supplements on admission without thinking about refeeding.
candidates.gain: The threshold and the first steps.
candidates.follow: Precise teaching on a harm that is easy to prevent.
candidates.earlier_overlap: none

candidates.working_title: Unexplained weight loss after 60 deserves a measured weight and a plan
candidates.core_insight: In pooled primary care studies, weight loss recorded by a GP in someone aged 60 or over carried a cancer risk above the 3 in 100 level UK guidance uses to prompt investigation, yet most studies relied on a coded symptom rather than a measured weight.
candidates.angle: Two lessons from one review: take recorded weight loss seriously and look widely (several cancer sites and many non-cancer causes), and weigh people so the loss is measured. How far to investigate follows the person's goals.
candidates.position: Unexplained weight loss in an older person should prompt a measured weight, a broad assessment (cancer, teeth and swallowing, mood, medicines, thyroid and diabetes, money and food access, living alone) and investigations in proportion to the person's wishes.
claims_needing_evidence: A systematic review of 25 primary care studies found weight loss was associated with 10 cancer sites, and the positive predictive value for cancer exceeded 3% in men and women aged 60 and over (Nicholson 2018).
20 of the 25 studies defined weight loss as a clinician's coded symptom; one used objective measurements (Nicholson 2018).
UK suspected cancer guidance uses a 3% positive predictive value threshold to recommend investigation (NICE NG12).
Non-cancer causes of weight loss in older people are common (clinical review).
evidence_leads: Nicholson BD et al. Br J Gen Pract 2018;68:e311-22. PMID 29632004 (abstract read on PubMed in this session).
NICE NG12. Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, updated) (official; not openable here).
Gaddey HL, Holder KK. Unintentional weight loss in older adults. Am Fam Physician (2014 or 2021) (unsure).
candidates.opening_line_draft: Weight loss recorded by a GP in someone aged 60 or over carried a cancer risk above 3 in 100 in pooled primary care studies.
candidates.visual_idea: Diagram: 'Unexplained weight loss' at the centre with spokes to cancer (several sites), mouth and teeth, swallowing, mood, medicines, thyroid and diabetes, money and food access, living alone. Footer: 'Weigh, record, compare.' Credit: Nicholson et al., BJGP 2018.
candidates.pause: GPs who see weight loss as vague.
candidates.gain: A reason to act, a list of causes and a reminder to measure.
candidates.follow: Careful reading of a review, including its limitation.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E126 (weight loss as a frailty sign, for families). This differs: the diagnostic meaning of weight loss for clinicians.

candidates.working_title: When food tastes of nothing
candidates.core_insight: Sense of smell declines markedly in later life, which helps explain why food can seem bland; stronger flavours, varied textures and a check of medicines and the mouth can help.
candidates.angle: Loss of interest in food is often put down to fussiness or low mood. Much of what we call taste comes from smell, and more than half of people aged 65 to 80 in a large study had a major loss of smell.
candidates.position: Explanatory, with practical suggestions: add flavour with herbs, spices, sauces and sharp tastes, vary textures and temperatures, and ask whether medicines or mouth problems are affecting taste.
claims_needing_evidence: In 1955 people aged 5 to 99, more than half of those aged 65 to 80 and more than three-quarters of those over 80 had major impairment of smell identification (Doty 1984).
Many medicines can alter taste or smell (clinical review; see leads).
Flavour enhancement of food has shown mixed effects on intake in older people (trials; check before making any claim of benefit).
evidence_leads: Doty RL et al. Smell identification ability: changes with age. Science 1984;226:1441-3. PMID 6505700 (abstract read on PubMed in this session).
Schiffman SS. Taste and smell losses in normal aging and disease. JAMA 1997;278:1357-62 (unsure).
Mathey MF et al. Flavor enhancement of food improves dietary intake and nutritional status of elderly nursing home residents. J Gerontol A 2001 (unsure).
