candidates.working_title: Could a medicine be drying your mouth?
candidates.core_insight: Many medicines taken in later life reduce saliva, and a dry mouth makes chewing, swallowing, wearing dentures and tasting harder and raises the risk of tooth decay, so it is worth asking for a review.
candidates.angle: Dry mouth is often dismissed as part of ageing. A meta-analysis found bladder medicines, antidepressants and some psychiatric medicines were linked with dry mouth, and so was the number of medicines taken.
candidates.position: If your mouth is often dry, ask your GP or pharmacist whether a medicine could be the cause and whether each medicine is still needed; meanwhile use water, sugar-free gum or saliva sprays rather than sugary sweets.
claims_needing_evidence: In a systematic review and meta-analysis of studies in people aged 60 and over, urological medicines, antidepressants and psycholeptics were associated with dry mouth in intervention studies, and the number of medicines was associated with dry mouth in observational studies (Tan 2018).
The risk of dry mouth was greatest for drugs used for urinary incontinence (Tan 2018 abstract).
Saliva protects teeth, and a dry mouth increases the risk of decay (dental guidance; see leads).
Sucking sugary sweets to relieve dryness increases decay risk (dental guidance).
evidence_leads: Tan ECK et al. Medications that cause dry mouth as an adverse effect in older people: a systematic review and metaanalysis. J Am Geriatr Soc 2018;66:76-84. PMID 29071719 (abstract read on PubMed in this session).
Office for Health Improvement and Disparities. Delivering better oral health, version 4 (2021) (official; check dry mouth section).
Thomson WM. Dry mouth and older people. Aust Dent J 2015 (unsure).
candidates.opening_line_draft: If your mouth is often dry, ask whether one of your medicines could be the cause.
candidates.visual_idea: Question card: 'Ask your GP or pharmacist: Could any of my medicines cause a dry mouth? Is each one still needed? Is there an alternative?' Below: 'Meanwhile: sips of water, sugar-free gum, saliva spray. Avoid sucking sugary sweets.'
candidates.pause: Older people with a dry mouth who were told it is their age.
candidates.gain: Three questions and safe relief measures.
candidates.follow: Links everyday symptoms to medicines in a practical way.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E141 (bladder antimuscarinics and cognition). This differs: the effect on the mouth, eating and teeth.

candidates.working_title: More older people keep their own teeth, and mouth care has to change
candidates.core_insight: Far fewer older people have no natural teeth than a generation ago, so carers and care homes increasingly need to clean natural teeth, crowns and bridges for someone else, not only dentures.
candidates.angle: The picture of mouth care as a denture pot is out of date for many people now receiving care. Natural teeth in a person who depends on others can decay quickly, especially at the roots, and brushing another person's teeth is a skill that needs teaching.
candidates.position: Care home and home care training should include brushing natural teeth for another person, and residents with their own teeth should have regular dental review.
claims_needing_evidence: The proportion of adults in England, Wales and Northern Ireland with no natural teeth fell from [N to verify] in 1968 to [N to verify] in 2009 (Adult Dental Health Survey 2009).
Among the oldest age groups, the proportion with some natural teeth has risen (Adult Dental Health Survey 2009 or Adult Oral Health Survey 2021; figures to verify).
NICE recommends an oral health assessment on admission to a care home and daily support with brushing natural teeth and cleaning dentures (NICE NG48, 2016).
High-fluoride toothpaste is recommended for adults at high risk of decay (Delivering better oral health, 2021).
evidence_leads: Health and Social Care Information Centre. Adult Dental Health Survey 2009, summary report (2011) (official; figures unsure).
Office for Health Improvement and Disparities. Adult Oral Health Survey 2021 (published 2023 to 2024) (unsure).
NICE NG48. Oral health for adults in care homes (2016) (official).
Office for Health Improvement and Disparities. Delivering better oral health, version 4 (2021) (official).
candidates.opening_line_draft: Brushing another person's natural teeth is a different skill from cleaning their dentures, and care homes now need both.
candidates.visual_idea: Accurate bar chart, if the survey figures are verified: percentage of adults with no natural teeth at each Adult Dental Health Survey year, labelled with years and source. Second slide: a short checklist for brushing someone else's teeth (stand or sit where you can see, small soft brush, pea-sized fluoride toothpaste, spit rather than rinse).
candidates.pause: Care workers trained mainly on dentures.
candidates.gain: A reason to update training and a short technique list.
candidates.follow: Uses population data to explain a change in everyday care.
candidates.earlier_overlap: none

candidates.working_title: When someone with dementia pushes the toothbrush away
candidates.core_insight: A relationship-based approach tested in a randomised trial helped more nursing home residents with dementia accept mouth care, using techniques families and care workers can learn.
candidates.angle: Refusing mouth care is often a response to feeling threatened. Reducing the threat (approaching at eye level, explaining, letting the person hold the brush, starting the movement and letting them carry on) made mouth care more likely to happen.
candidates.position: When a person with dementia resists mouth care, change the approach before concluding that brushing isn't possible.
claims_needing_evidence: In a randomised trial of 101 nursing home residents with dementia who resisted mouth care, the MOUTh intervention gave twice the odds of allowing mouth care and completing oral hygiene, with longer mouth care, small reductions in resistance and small improvements in oral health (Jablonski 2018); for the public, state this as 'more residents accepted mouth care'.

MOUTh techniques include approaching at eye level, smiling, using gestures, bridging (giving the person an object such as a toothbrush to hold), chaining (starting a task and letting the person continue), hand-over-hand guidance and distraction (intervention description paper needed).
The trial authors concluded that managing refusal may be more realistic than eliminating it (Jablonski 2018 abstract).
evidence_leads: Jablonski RA et al. Randomised clinical trial: efficacy of strategies to provide oral hygiene activities to nursing home residents with dementia who resist mouth care. Gerodontology 2018;35:365-75. PMID 30004139 (abstract read on PubMed in this session).
Jablonski RA et al. Reducing care-resistant behaviors during oral hygiene in persons with dementia. BMC Oral Health 2011 (unsure; likely describes the techniques).
Zimmerman S et al. JAMA Netw Open 2020, PMID 32558913 (a different programme, Mouth Care Without a Battle; do not confuse).
candidates.opening_line_draft: A gentler way of starting mouth care helped more nursing home residents with dementia accept having their teeth cleaned, in a US trial.
candidates.visual_idea: Four-panel comic strip, labelled as illustrative: 1, a carer approaches from behind with a brush and the person flinches ('less helpful'); 2, the carer comes round to eye level and says what they will do; 3, the carer hands the person a toothbrush and stands beside them at the mirror; 4, the carer gently guides the person's hand. No attributed quotations.
candidates.pause: Carers who have given up on brushing a parent's teeth.
candidates.gain: Techniques to try tonight.
candidates.follow: Shows good care in concrete steps.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E061 (resistance to care is often fear of the unannounced; warn, ask, explain). This differs: mouth care specifically, with trial evidence and named techniques.

candidates.working_title: Take the dentures out at night
candidates.core_insight: In a study of people aged 85 and over, those who slept in their dentures had a higher rate of pneumonia, and more plaque and yeast in the mouth, than those who took them out.
candidates.angle: A small nightly habit with a measurable association. Add two related details: clean the dentures daily, and mark them with the person's name before a hospital stay.
candidates.position: Unless a dentist advises otherwise, take dentures out at night, clean them, and store them as the dentist advises; label them before a hospital stay. The pneumonia finding is an association, not proof of cause.
claims_needing_evidence: In 524 community-living people aged 85 and over in Tokyo (453 denture wearers), 40.8% of denture wearers wore them during sleep; overnight wearing was independently associated with a higher incidence of pneumonia over 3 years (Iinuma 2015; state as 'linked with a higher risk', not 'doubles').
People who wore dentures overnight had more tongue and denture plaque, gum inflammation and Candida (Iinuma 2015).
Standard dental advice is to remove dentures at night (NHS or dental association guidance).
Dentures are sometimes lost during hospital stays (needs a source such as NHS Resolution or an audit; drop if none).
evidence_leads: Iinuma T et al. Denture wearing during sleep doubles the risk of pneumonia in the very elderly. J Dent Res 2015;94(3 Suppl):28S-36S. PMID 25294364 (abstract read on PubMed in this session).
NHS website guidance on dentures care (official; not openable here).
Oral Health Foundation denture care advice (unsure).
candidates.opening_line_draft: Sleeping in dentures was linked with a higher risk of pneumonia in a study of people aged 85 and over.
candidates.visual_idea: Statement card with a small checklist: 'Out at night. Brushed, not only soaked. Stored as your dentist advises. Name marked on them before a hospital stay.' A drawn denture case on a bedside table. Credit: Iinuma et al., J Dent Res 2015.
candidates.pause: Denture wearers and carers who never thought about night-time wearing.
candidates.gain: A nightly habit and a hospital tip.
candidates.follow: Small, concrete, evidence-linked advice.
candidates.earlier_overlap: none

candidates.working_title: Losing weight after 65: keep the muscle
candidates.core_insight: In a trial of older adults with obesity, weight loss combined with both strength and aerobic exercise improved physical function most, and aerobic exercise alone lost the most muscle and hip bone.
candidates.angle: Weight loss in later life can remove muscle and bone along with fat, and the type of exercise changed how much. ESPEN advises weight-reducing diets only for older people with weight-related health problems, and always with exercise.
candidates.position: When weight loss is appropriate for an older person, it should be combined with strength exercise and adequate protein and planned around function.
claims_needing_evidence: In 160 adults aged 65 and over with obesity, randomised for 6 months, body weight fell by about 9% in all exercise groups (Villareal 2017).

Lean mass fell by 5% with aerobic exercise alone, compared with 2% with resistance and 3% with combined training; hip bone density fell by 3% with aerobic alone compared with 0.5% to 1% in the other groups (Villareal 2017).
Physical Performance Test scores improved most with combined aerobic and resistance training (21%, compared with 14% in each single-exercise group) (Villareal 2017).
ESPEN recommends weight-reducing diets only in older people with obesity and weight-related health problems, combined with physical exercise (ESPEN 2019 abstract).
evidence_leads: Villareal DT et al. Aerobic or resistance exercise, or both, in dieting obese older adults. N Engl J Med 2017;376:1943-55. PMID 28514618 (abstract read on PubMed in this session).
Volkert D et al. ESPEN guideline on clinical nutrition and hydration in geriatrics. Clin Nutr 2019;38:10-47 (abstract wording confirmed via the 2026 translation, PMID 41820196).
candidates.opening_line_draft: Older adults with obesity lost about 9% of their weight in a six-month trial whichever exercise they did. Those doing aerobic exercise alone lost the most muscle.
candidates.visual_idea: Accurate bar chart: change in lean mass after 6 months by group (aerobic 5% loss, resistance 2% loss, combined 3% loss), labelled with n=160 randomised, 141 completed, and credit Villareal et al., NEJM 2017. A second slide lists 'Strength exercise, enough protein, a goal about function'.
candidates.pause: Older people advised to lose weight, and clinicians prescribing weight loss.
candidates.gain: Trial evidence on how to lose weight without losing strength.
candidates.follow: Evidence on a current question for older people, read carefully.
candidates.earlier_overlap: none (C02 may cover muscle loss; this is about intentional weight loss).

candidates.working_title: A prescribed supplement only helps once it is drunk
candidates.core_insight: People drink more of their prescribed nutrition supplements in the community than in hospital, and more when the supplements are energy-dense; records should show what was drunk, not only what was prescribed.
candidates.angle: The prescription chart shows two bottles a day; the locker may show two unopened bottles. Smaller, energy-dense formats, offered between meals at set times by a named person, with intake recorded, turn a prescription into nutrition.
candidates.position: Supplement plans should specify the format, the times, who offers it and how intake is recorded, with regular review.
claims_needing_evidence: Across 46 studies (4328 people), mean compliance with oral nutritional supplements was 78%: 67% in hospital and 81% in the community (Hubbard 2012).
Higher energy density was associated with higher compliance (Hubbard 2012; association across unmatched studies).
The lead author worked for a supplement manufacturer (declare in the evidence record, not in the post).
Offering small supplement volumes with medicine rounds increases intake (needs a study; drop if not found).
evidence_leads: Hubbard GP et al. A systematic review of compliance to oral nutritional supplements. Clin Nutr 2012;31:293-312. PMID 22257636 (abstract read on PubMed in this session).
Doll-Shankaruk M et al. Implementation and effects of a medication pass nutritional supplement program in a long-term care facility. J Gerontol Nurs 2008 (unsure).
NICE CG32 on reviewing oral nutrition support (official).
candidates.opening_line_draft: About two-thirds of prescribed supplement drinks were actually drunk in hospital studies [verify: 67%, Hubbard 2012].
candidates.visual_idea: Comparison card: 'Prescribed: two bottles a day' beside 'What helps them get drunk': smaller energy-dense format; offered between meals; a flavour the person likes; someone opens it; intake written down. Labelled 'Illustrative example' for the prescription.
candidates.pause: Nurses who return unopened bottles every day.
candidates.gain: Concrete changes that raise intake.
candidates.follow: Attention to what happens after the prescription.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E108 (protein left on the tray after hip fracture). This differs: supplement practicalities.

candidates.working_title: Hospital nutrition support has trial evidence: what EFFORT showed
candidates.core_insight: In a large Swiss trial of medical inpatients at nutritional risk, individualised nutrition support started within 48 hours reduced adverse outcomes and deaths at 30 days compared with standard hospital food.
candidates.angle: Nutrition in hospital is often treated as hospitality. EFFORT is randomised evidence that planned, dietitian-led support changes outcomes. The post should also say what it did not test: supplements alone without a dietitian, long-term outcomes, and UK or care home settings.
candidates.position: Screening for malnutrition should lead to individualised support started early; screening without action is incomplete.
claims_needing_evidence: 2088 medical inpatients at nutritional risk (NRS 2002 score 3 or more) in eight Swiss hospitals were randomised to individualised support or standard hospital food (Schuetz 2019).
By 30 days, 23% of the intervention group and 27% of the control group had an adverse outcome, and 7% and 10% had died (Schuetz 2019).
Calorie goals were reached in 79% and protein goals in 76% of the intervention group; the trial was open-label (Schuetz 2019).
The age profile of participants (to verify in full text) before claiming relevance to older people.
evidence_leads: Schuetz P et al. Individualised nutritional support in medical inpatients at nutritional risk: a randomised clinical trial. Lancet 2019;393:2312-21. PMID 31030981 (abstract read on PubMed in this session).
EFFORT secondary analyses in older or frail participants (unsure).
candidates.opening_line_draft: Seven in 100 medical inpatients given individualised nutrition support had died by 30 days, compared with 10 in 100 given standard hospital food, in a trial of 2,088 people.
candidates.visual_idea: Icon array: two panels of 100 figures, highlighting 7 and 10 deaths by 30 days, with a second pair for adverse outcomes (23 and 27). Credit: Schuetz et al., Lancet 2019; label 'medical inpatients at nutritional risk, 8 Swiss hospitals'.
candidates.pause: Clinicians who doubt that nutrition changes hard outcomes.
candidates.gain: Absolute numbers from a large trial, with its limits.
candidates.follow: Careful trial reading in plain numbers.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E108 (nutrition after hip fracture is treatment). This differs: interpretation of a general medical inpatient trial.

candidates.working_title: Who checks the teeth of people who can't get to a dentist?
candidates.core_insight: People living in care homes or unable to leave home often go without routine dental checks, and a national review in England found oral health often missing from care home care plans.
candidates.angle: Families assume someone is looking after the mouth. National guidance expects an oral health assessment on admission and daily support; asking three questions shows whether it is happening.
candidates.position: Care homes should assess oral health on admission, support daily mouth care and arrange dental care for residents who can't travel; families can ask how this is done. This follows NICE guidance and takes no position on dental funding.
claims_needing_evidence: A 2019 CQC review of care homes in England found that [N to verify] of care plans reviewed did not cover, or only partly covered, oral health, and that many homes had no oral health policy or staff training (official report; figures to verify).
NICE recommends that care home residents have an oral health assessment on admission, recorded in the care plan, with daily support for mouth care (NICE NG48, 2016).
Scotland runs a national oral health training programme for care home staff (Caring for Smiles; official; check).
evidence_leads: Care Quality Commission. 'Smiling matters': oral health care in care homes (2019) (official report title; figures unsure; web pages not openable here).
NICE NG48. Oral health for adults in care homes (2016) (official).
Public Health Scotland / NHS Education for Scotland. Caring for Smiles programme materials (unsure).
candidates.opening_line_draft: Ask the care home when your mother's mouth was last checked, and by whom.
candidates.visual_idea: Question card with three questions: Was her mouth checked when she moved in? Who helps her clean her teeth or dentures each day? How does she see a dentist if she can't travel?
candidates.pause: Families who have never thought to ask about teeth in a care home.
candidates.gain: Three questions that reveal whether mouth care is happening.
candidates.follow: Draws attention to a group easily overlooked.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E022 (ask for a diagnostic review in a care home). This differs: oral health and dental access.

candidates.working_title: Sharing the serving dish
candidates.core_insight: In a Dutch trial, nursing home residents who ate family style, serving themselves from dishes at a shared table, kept their weight and quality of life better than those given pre-plated meals.
candidates.angle: A change of routine rather than a product: the meal as a shared occasion with choice. The trial included residents without dementia, which the post should say.
candidates.position: Care homes and wards could offer shared-table, self-serve meals for people able to take part; a cluster randomised trial supports this for residents without dementia.
claims_needing_evidence: In five Dutch nursing homes, 178 residents without dementia (mean age 77) were cluster randomised by ward to family style meals or usual pre-plated service for six months (Nijs 2006).
Compared with control, the family style group had a relative gain in overall quality of life (6.1 units), fine motor function and body weight (1.5 kg) (Nijs 2006).
Evidence for residents with dementia is less clear (needs a source; state as a limitation).
evidence_leads: Nijs KA et al. Effect of family style mealtimes on quality of life, physical performance, and body weight of nursing home residents: cluster randomised controlled trial. BMJ 2006;332:1180-4. PMID 16679331 (abstract read on PubMed in this session).
de Castro JM. Family and friends produce greater social facilitation of food intake than other companions. Physiol Behav 1994 (unsure).
Charras K, Fremontier M. Sharing meals with institutionalized people with dementia: a natural experiment. J Gerontol Soc Work 2010 (unsure).
candidates.opening_line_draft: Residents of Dutch nursing homes who served themselves from shared dishes kept more weight over six months than residents given plated meals.
candidates.visual_idea: Drawn illustration: residents at a table passing a dish of vegetables, one using a walking frame parked nearby. A small result panel: 'Over 6 months, compared with plated meals: better quality of life scores; weight about 1.5 kg higher. Nijs et al., BMJ 2006. Residents without dementia.'
candidates.pause: Care home staff and families who picture meals as trays.
candidates.gain: A trial-backed change in routine.
candidates.follow: Positive, specific examples of care that works.

candidates.working_title: Red plates for dementia: what the study was
candidates.core_insight: The best-known study behind red plates for people with dementia included nine men; the idea is cheap and low risk to try, but it is not established and it doesn't replace help with eating.
candidates.angle: A popular tip read against its source: nine men with advanced Alzheimer's in one facility, ten days per condition, more eaten and drunk with high-contrast tableware, and a follow-up showing high-contrast blue also worked. The finding is about contrast, not the colour red.
candidates.position: High-contrast tableware is reasonable to try because it is cheap and harmless, but services should not present it as proven or count it in place of mealtime help.
claims_needing_evidence: Nine men with advanced Alzheimer's disease in long-term care ate 25% more food and drank 84% more liquid, on average, with high-contrast red tableware than with white; 8 of 9 increased intake (Dunne 2004).
In a follow-up a year later, high-contrast blue tableware also increased intake, while low-contrast red and low-contrast blue did not (Dunne 2004).
No large trials have confirmed the effect (needs a systematic review of mealtime interventions in dementia).
evidence_leads: Dunne TE et al. Visual contrast enhances food and liquid intake in advanced Alzheimer's disease. Clin Nutr 2004;23:533-8. PMID 15297089 (abstract read on PubMed in this session).
Abdelhamid A et al. Effectiveness of interventions to directly support food and drink intake in people with dementia: systematic review and meta-analysis. BMC Geriatr 2016 (unsure).
candidates.opening_line_draft: The best-known study behind red plates for people with dementia included nine men.
candidates.visual_idea: Annotated evidence card: 'What the study was: 9 men; advanced Alzheimer's; one care facility; 10 days each of white, red, then white plates. Found: more eaten and drunk with high-contrast plates. Follow-up: high-contrast blue also worked; low-contrast red did not.' Credit: Dunne et al., Clin Nutr 2004.
candidates.pause: Anyone who has shared or bought red plates.
candidates.gain: A fair reading of a popular tip.
candidates.follow: Reads evidence behind widely shared advice.
candidates.earlier_overlap: none

candidates.working_title: Plain water between meals for people on thickened drinks
candidates.core_insight: For carefully selected people on thickened drinks, allowing plain water between meals after mouth care did not increase lung complications in rehabilitation studies, and may increase how much they drink.
candidates.angle: Thickened drinks reduce aspiration on imaging but are linked with people drinking less. The free water protocol accepts a small amount of water aspiration from a clean mouth in exchange for better hydration and satisfaction, with strict selection.
candidates.position: Teams could consider a free water protocol for selected patients in rehabilitation settings with strict criteria and good mouth care; the evidence is low quality and doesn't extend to everyone.
claims_needing_evidence: A systematic review of 8 studies (215 rehabilitation and 30 acute inpatients) found low-quality evidence that the free water protocol did not increase the odds of lung complications, and low-quality evidence that fluid intake may increase (Gillman 2017).
Patients' swallow-related quality of life appeared to improve (Gillman 2017).
The review concluded the protocol can be offered to carefully selected adult rehabilitation inpatients, with strict exclusion criteria including cognition and mobility (Gillman 2017).
Thickened liquids were linked with more dehydration than chin-down posture in a randomised trial (Robbins 2008).
evidence_leads: Gillman A, Winkler R, Taylor NF. Implementing the free water protocol does not result in aspiration pneumonia in carefully selected patients with dysphagia: a systematic review. Dysphagia 2017;32:345-61. PMID 27878598 (abstract read on PubMed in this session).
Robbins J et al. Ann Intern Med 2008;148:509-18. PMID 18378947 (abstract read on PubMed in this session).
Panther K. The Frazier free water protocol. Perspectives on Swallowing and Swallowing Disorders 2005 (unsure).
candidates.opening_line_draft: Some rehabilitation units let selected patients on thickened drinks have plain water between meals, after mouth care.
candidates.visual_idea: Decision diagram: 'Could this person be suitable?' with the protocol's selection points (to be taken from the source), then steps: mouth care first; water between meals only; review. Clearly states 'rehabilitation settings; low-quality evidence'.
candidates.pause: Therapists and nurses who see people on thickened drinks drinking very little.
candidates.gain: A structured option and its evidence limits.
candidates.follow: Open discussion of a real trade-off.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E187 (do not thicken and miss the pneumonia). This differs: an alternative to thickening for selected people.

candidates.working_title: The 'diabetic diet' for someone who is frail and losing weight
candidates.core_insight: For frail older people with diabetes who are eating poorly, restricting sugar and portions adds risks of undernutrition and low blood sugar; guidance advises relaxing dietary restrictions and adjusting medicines to what the person eats.
candidates.angle: A shortcut that needs qualifying: 'diabetes means a restricted diet'. In frailty and in care homes, the goals shift towards eating enough and avoiding hypoglycaemia.
candidates.position: In frail older people with diabetes and poor intake, avoid restrictive diets and match glucose-lowering medicines to actual intake, with agreed glucose targets.
claims_needing_evidence: ESPEN advises that dietary restrictions should generally be avoided in older people (ESPEN 2019 abstract).

International and UK guidance for older people with diabetes in care homes recommends individualised targets and avoiding restrictive diets (Diabetes UK 2010 care home guidance; ADA Standards of Care older adults section; to confirm wording).
Hypoglycaemia risk rises when intake falls in people taking insulin or sulfonylureas (clinical review).

American Diabetes Association. Standards of Care in Diabetes, section 13, Older Adults (current year) (unsure of exact wording).
Diabetes UK. Good clinical practice guidelines for care home residents with diabetes (2010) (unsure).
Dorner B, Friedrich EK. Position of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics: individualized nutrition approaches for older adults. J Acad Nutr Diet (2016 or 2018) (unsure).
candidates.opening_line_draft: For a frail older person with diabetes who is eating less and losing weight, a restrictive 'diabetic diet' adds risk.
candidates.visual_idea: Comparison card: 'Restrictive diet' (smaller, sugar-free meals; less eaten; low blood sugar if medicines unchanged) beside 'Individual plan' (usual foods; regular meals and snacks; medicines matched to intake; targets agreed with the person).
candidates.pause: Care home staff and clinicians who still apply diabetic diets to frail residents.
candidates.gain: A corrected default and what to do instead.
candidates.follow: Teaching that fits treatment to the person in front of you.

candidates.working_title: 38 minutes per meal
candidates.core_insight: In a US nursing home study, one-to-one help with a meal took an average of 38 minutes per resident, compared with about 9 minutes of help in usual care, and half of residents ate more with that help.
candidates.angle: Staffing plans count people on shift. They rarely count the minutes it takes to help one person eat. When the minutes aren't there, care workers are not failing; the plan is.
candidates.position: Mealtime staffing should be planned from how many people need help and how long help takes. This is about the conditions of care work, not individual effort, and takes no position on specific staffing ratios.
claims_needing_evidence: In 74 residents of three US nursing homes given a two-day, six-meal trial of one-to-one feeding assistance, half significantly increased food and fluid intake (Simmons 2001).
The assistance took an average of 38 minutes per resident per meal, compared with 9 minutes provided by staff in usual care (Simmons 2001).
The study is small, from 2001 and from the US; UK staffing may differ (state as a limitation).
evidence_leads: Simmons SF, Osterweil D, Schnelle JF. Improving food intake in nursing home residents with feeding assistance: a staffing analysis. J Gerontol A 2001;56:M790-4. PMID 11723156 (abstract read on PubMed in this session).
Simmons SF, Schnelle JF. Feeding assistance needs of long-stay nursing home residents and staff time to provide care. J Am Geriatr Soc 2006 (unsure).
candidates.opening_line_draft: In a US nursing home study, one-to-one help with a meal took an average of 38 minutes per resident. Usual care provided about 9.
candidates.visual_idea: Accurate bar chart: 9 minutes (usual care) and 38 minutes (one-to-one assistance) per resident per meal, labelled, with 'Simmons et al., 2001; 74 residents; 3 US nursing homes'. Second slide: 'Half of residents ate more with this help.'
candidates.pause: Care workers who know they can't give each person the time they need.
